title: “Always AI-free” says iStock – before immediately encouraging you to AI-edit its photos!
source_used: Digital Camera World (pre-fetched full text; first-person opinion piece)
key_facts: Ariane Sherine Juniper, writing in Digital Camera World, describes buying photos from the stock library iStock (iStockPhoto), which is owned by Getty Images, for $125 / £142.80 a month for 50 downloads.
iStock tells her it is 'always AI free' and allows no AI-generated visuals in its library.
As soon as she buys a photo, iStock invites her to 'customise this image' with AI.
Following that prompt removes the photo's background; a separate text box ('What would you like to change?') lets the user ask for other changes, such as turning a plant green.
She tested the tool by asking it to turn a bath bright pink and says the result was very convincing.
She calls the mix comical and says stock libraries are trying to please creators who resent AI and customers who use it, while not falling behind rivals that use AI.
The piece carries no reply from iStock or Getty Images.
quote_evidence: Which is kind of hilarious, because as soon as you purchase a photo, iStockPhoto encourages you to "customise this image" using AI!
Type in, for example, "Change the plant to green" and hit "Modify."

Stock image companies don't know which section of the population to appease and pander to, but more than anything, they don't want to be left behind by other photo libraries using AI to their advantage.
why_it_matters_hint: Buyers and photographers may read 'AI free' as covering the whole service, but as quoted the promise is about the images in the library, not the editing tools.
event_date: Not stated; a personal opinion piece published 10 Oct 2026 about the writer's current use of the service.
notes: One writer's personal test, not a study; no response from iStock. The quoted promise ('doesn't allow any AI-generated visuals in our library') concerns the library's pictures, so calling the editing tool a contradiction is the writer's framing.
